note: Guided stories. Each step picks a place, a layer and a frame ('first', 'last', 'event' or a number).

steps.text: On June 24, 2026, two large earthquakes struck near Venezuela's coast. NISAR passed overhead before and after, 12 days apart.
Each rainbow band is about 12 cm of ground movement. Where bands crowd together, the ground shifted most over a short distance.
Twelve days later the ground was almost still. One sudden jump, then quiet: this place dances the Tango.
Mexico City sits on old lake clay. Pumping groundwater squeezes the clay, and the city slowly sinks.
Watch the bowl deepen pass after pass. A steady trend in one direction: this place dances the March.
The speed map shows where sinking is fastest. GNSS stations on the ground check the radar's numbers.
In the dry season, Tonle Sap is a modest lake in the middle of Cambodia.
Monsoon rains push the Mekong so high that the river flows backwards and the lake swells several times over.
This is what the radar actually sees: calm water is dark, and flooded forest glows bright from double bounce. Clouds make no difference.
Shisper Glacier in Pakistan's Karakoram has surged before, damming a lake and setting off floods.
Pair after pair, the ice moves faster: a Crescendo. Tracking that speed-up gives people downstream time to prepare.
